claims.source: Unsolved Mysteries (NBC, 1990); 'The New Roswell: Kecksburg Exposed' (Sci Fi Channel, 2003)
claims.text: Kecksburg residents interviewed over four decades describe an object shaped like an acorn and about the size of a Volkswagen bearing writing resembling hieroglyphs, removed from the woods by a military operation; resident John Hays has stated since 1990 that as a ten-year-old he saw a flat-bed truck emerging from the site carrying something 'the size of a VW'.

The Greensburg Tribune-Review reported at the time that the landing area was immediately sealed off on the order of US Army and State Police officials in anticipation of a close inspection, and that state police ordered the area roped off pending the arrival of Army engineers and possibly civilian scientists; a subsequent edition ran the headline 'Searchers Fail to Find Object'.

claims.source: Inference from the Tribune-Review reporting set against the Kean v. NASA record
claims.text: The Kecksburg record is the domain's clearest instance of a documented cordon with an undocumented object: the sealing of the area is in the contemporary press, and the disposition of whatever was inside the cordon is in no released record of any agency. Reasoning: the cordon is tier 1, the object is tier 2 at best, and NASA has been judicially found not to have adequately searched for the difference.

conflicts: Astronomers Paul Annear, George Wetherill, William P. Bidelman and Fred Hess assessed the 1965 fireball as a meteor bolide; a 1967 Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada triangulation put the trajectory ending over western Lake Erie. NASA's 2005 statement attributed examined fragments to a Soviet satellite while stating the records were lost. NASA's own later position is that Cosmos 96 could not have been responsible.

label: Stan Gordon
narrative: Stan Gordon is the field researcher who kept Kecksburg alive for four decades until it reached a federal courtroom. A western Pennsylvania investigator who was a teenager in Greensburg when the fireball came down on 9 December 1965, he spent the following decades locating and interviewing local witnesses - residents who described a military and state police cordon thrown around the woods, a flatbed truck leaving the site carrying something acorn-shaped and about the size of a Volkswagen, and men in unmarked vehicles - while the official position remained that searchers found absolutely nothing. His witness pool supplied the 1990 Unsolved Mysteries episode, the 2003 Sci Fi Channel documentary 'The New Roswell: Kecksburg Exposed', and, indirectly, the evidentiary basis for Leslie Kean's 2003 FOIA request and lawsuit against NASA. Gordon's work is the standard illustration of the retrieval literature's characteristic profile: a large, internally consistent body of local first-hand testimony describing a recovery operation, and no document. The Kean litigation was the attempt to close that gap by force of law, and it produced a federal finding that NASA's searches were inadequate and sworn testimony that two boxes of records from the period were missing - not the object, but the paper trail of its absence.
